title: The Crest
scene: A sentence about today sounds like a decision about them.

paragraphs: "What happens if I don't?"
"Don't what?"
"Stay strong."
He let go of the frame. She set it down and checked the corner.
"I didn't mean you couldn't be upset."
"Then stop telling me how to do it."
Mukund looked away.
She reached for the glass and knocked it against the table's edge. Water spread over the top invitation. She caught the glass upright.
He picked up a cloth.
"Leave it."
"Aarna, it's water."
"I know what it is."
He put the cloth beside the glass. She stared at it, suddenly ashamed of the sound of her own voice.
"I'm not..." She wiped her palms on her trousers. "I can't keep doing this."
"Doing what?"
"Explaining. Every time I start to say something, you're already somewhere else."
"I'm right here."
"Then look at me."
He did.
For a moment she could not say anything. His face was so familiar that she had expected it to help.
"I wanted you to come," she said. "Not bring me another job."
"You don't have to do anything."
"Except feel better."
He slid the wet invitation onto the cloth. Her name was still readable.
"I don't know what you want from me."
"I've been trying to tell you."
"I came. I sat down. You didn't want me to call anyone. Fine. Now I can't even..."
He stopped with his hand over the cloth.
Aarna pulled her chair out but did not sit.
"Forget it," she said.
"Don't do that."
"Do what?"
"Say nothing and make me guess."
She looked at the paintings. He heard himself take a breath through his teeth.
"Maybe I'm not the person you need."
The chair scraped as she let go of it.
"Is that what you're saying?"
"What?"
"About us."
"No."
She waited.
"I'm talking about this. Today."
"You said you're not the person I need."
He pressed a thumb against the blue mark on his cuff.
"I don't know how to help you today. That's what I meant."
"You could have said that."
He nodded once. She was still standing on the other side of the table.
She sat because her legs had begun to shake.
The cloth was soaked now. She folded a dry corner over the invitation and pressed it down.
"I wanted to be sad with you."
"I am sad."
"I can't tell."
He looked at her hand on the paper.
"I keep thinking I have to do something."
"You were doing something when you first got here."
"What?"
"Before you got up."
Outside, someone leaned on a car horn. She listened until it stopped.
"Don't tell me to be strong," she said. "I came to you to be weak for a while."
He moved his cup, although it was empty and out of the way.
"I thought people were going to see it," she said. "Not just pictures on my phone. The actual work. My dad's put the invitation in the window, and I haven't even told him."
Her voice failed on the last word. She cleared her throat.
"And you keep showing me rooms."
"I'm sorry."
She nodded, but could not look at him yet.
His phone lit up. He turned it over.
"I need a minute."
Her eyes went to his bag.
"In the kitchen," he said. "I'll come back."
She heard him put his phone on the counter. Then nothing.
